text: Lesson 14's network module lives in its own folder today, but once more than one project calls it, every caller needs a way to say give me version 1.2, not whatever gets pushed next. That's the identical problem Lesson 1's provider version constraint solved, applied one layer up — to a shared library of HCL instead of a shared cloud-provider plugin.

When a module comes from a registry, public or private, the module block takes a version argument directly, using the same constraint syntax as a provider. source becomes a registry address — host, org, name, provider — not a file path. terraform init resolves the matching release and records it in .terraform.lock.hcl, the same lock file Lesson 2 introduced for providers.

A module doesn't need a registry at all — it can source straight from Git. That matters because version only works for registry sources; a git source pins its version a different way, with a ref query parameter appended to the URL itself. git:: marks it as a repository, the double slash points at a subdirectory, and ref equals v1.2.0 is the actual pin — a tag, branch, or commit.

Without a pin, a change the module's author makes — a renamed variable, a dropped resource — lands silently in every caller the next time someone runs init with upgrade. Pinning means that only happens when a team deliberately decides to move to a new version and tests against it first, not by accident.

Terraform Cloud and Enterprise add a private module registry: an org-scoped catalog, visible only inside that organization, where internal modules publish the same way HashiCorp publishes public ones — by pushing a semantic-version git tag. It's called exactly like the public-registry example, just with the org's own registry host in source.

The real value isn't the publishing mechanics — it's that every team consumes one reviewed, versioned network module from one place, instead of each team keeping its own copy-pasted variant that quietly drifts. Next lesson puts three such modules together — network, compute, and database — wiring one module's outputs directly into another's inputs.
